meta.title: Music Theory for Songwriting & Arrangement
meta.interests: Practical mechanisms, music, space, technology and worked examples

plan.title: Music Theory for Songwriting & Arrangement
plan.hook: You can know every note in a scale and still struggle to write a memorable phrase. Start with a musical home, then shape harmony, rhythm and individual voices into an original eight-bar sketch.
objectives: Hear and describe tonal relationships using scale degrees and intervals
Choose chord functions and voice leading that support a phrase
Count durations, rests and chord changes in 4/4
Write and revise an eight-bar melody with a simple arrangement
prerequisites: Basic note names; an instrument or the ability to hum is helpful
Learnway’s Sound & Music explains the physical foundations

sections.heading: Hear a home note before naming the chords
points: Tonic: a tonal centre is a point of reference, not just the first note
Scale degrees: numbers describe notes relative to that centre
Major scale: whole and half steps create a reusable pattern
Intervals: describe the distance between notes
Experiment: change the ending while keeping the phrase unchanged

sections.heading: Give a progression somewhere to go
points: Triads: stack alternate scale tones to build three-note chords
Roman numerals: uppercase major and lowercase minor in this course
Function: tonic, predominant and dominant describe common tonal roles
Cadence: the ending of a phrase shapes its sense of arrival
Style: useful tendencies are not universal composition rules

sections.heading: Move the voices, not just the chord labels
points: Voicing: the same chord tones can occupy different registers and orders
Common tones: hold a shared note when it serves the phrase
Economy: compare small inner-voice moves with larger leaps
Bass role: a bass note can establish the root beneath an inversion
Independence: preserve audible parts and comfortable ranges

sections.heading: Make repetition feel intentional
points: Meter: group pulses so rhythmic placement has a reference
Duration: quarter notes, eighth notes and rests occupy time
Syncopation: emphasise an offbeat or carry sound across an expected accent
Groove: coordinate parts through a shared timing pattern
Space: leave deliberate gaps for melody, breath and contrast

sections.heading: Write a melody that asks and answers
points: Motive: a short recognisable idea can return with variation
Chord tones: use harmonic support without restricting every note
Passing motion: connect stable tones with purposeful non-chord tones
Contour: plan a high point and a place to settle
Phrasing: breath, rests and endings make the line feel intentional

sections.heading: Arrange an eight-bar song sketch
points: Form: plan two four-bar phrases with different endings
Harmony: give each bar a clear chord and count changes within bars
Melody: preserve a motive while shaping a peak and resolution
Arrangement: assign bass, harmony and melody distinct jobs
Revision: compare one controlled change at a time

sections.heading: Hear a home note before naming the chords
sections.body:
Play or hum C–D–E–G, then end on C. Repeat the same opening but end on B. In a C-major context, the second ending often feels less settled. That expectation is a useful starting point for theory: musical labels describe relationships you can test with your ears. They are not guarantees of the same emotional response in every style or listener.

The tonic is the perceived tonal centre. A major scale arranges seven different note names around that centre using whole step, whole step, half step, whole step, whole step, whole step, half step. On a keyboard, a half step is the distance to the next key, including black keys; a whole step is two half steps. C major uses C D E F G A B, returning to C an octave higher. Its half steps are E–F and B–C.

Scale degrees name these relationships with numbers: in C major, C is 1, D is 2, and B is 7. Transpose the same scale-degree pattern to G major and degree 7 becomes F-sharp, not F-natural. An interval describes the separation of two pitches; its number counts note names inclusively, while its quality specifies the more exact distance. C to E is a major third, four half steps.

**Predict:** Move C–E–G up two half steps while preserving the intervals. The result is D–F-sharp–A. D–F–A changes the middle interval and produces a minor triad instead.

**Try it:** Hum a short phrase, stop before its final note, and try two endings. Identify which sounds more settled in the context you created. Then write its scale degrees and transpose those relationships to another key. An instrument helps you check pitches, but the goal is to hear the relationship before treating the symbols as an answer.

questions.q: Why does C–E–G become D–F-sharp–A when transposed up two half steps?
questions.hint: Move every pitch by the same distance.
questions.answer: All three pitches move up two half steps, preserving the major-third and perfect-fifth relationships. D–F–A would change the third to minor.

questions.q: Is the first note of any melody necessarily the tonic?
questions.hint: Distinguish order of appearance from a sense of tonal centre.
questions.answer: No. The tonic is established by the musical context and sense of home; a melody may begin on another scale degree.

sections.heading: Give a progression somewhere to go
sections.body:
A chord progression can create a journey even when its chord vocabulary is small. In C major, build triads by stacking alternate notes from the scale: C–E–G, D–F–A, E–G–B, F–A–C, G–B–D, A–C–E and B–D–F. These are C major, D minor, E minor, F major, G major, A minor and B diminished.

Roman numerals describe their roots relative to the key. We use uppercase for major and lowercase for minor: I, ii, iii, IV, V and vi. The diminished triad is vii°. In this convention I in C major means C major, while vi means A minor. A chord symbol such as Am names a chord independently of its function in the current key.

In familiar major-key tonal music, I often provides rest, ii or IV can prepare a move away, and V can create an expectation of return. The B in the G-major chord (G–B–D) is the leading tone of C major and tends toward C in that context. Adding F creates G7, whose B and F can resolve to C and E. This is a useful tendency, not an obligation for every voice in every genre.

**Compare:** I–vi–IV–V, or C–Am–F–G, ends on a dominant chord. Add I and the phrase gains a more settled return. V–vi instead can defer the expected arrival. Many popular songs use repeated loops whose effect depends on melody, rhythm and production, so do not grade every song against a single classical cadence template.

**Try it:** Play or imagine C–Am–F–G twice. On one repetition, stop on G; on the next, add C. Describe the difference before naming it. Then change only the final chord and decide whether the new ending supports the phrase you want.
sections.visual: In C major, the same chords can be labelled by name and by scale-degree role. The final move from G to C is one common dominant-to-tonic arrival.

questions.q: What does vi mean in C major using this course’s convention?
questions.hint: Count six scale degrees, then build the diatonic triad.
questions.answer: It means A minor: A–C–E. The lowercase numeral indicates minor quality.

questions.q: Why might C–Am–F–G sound less finished than C–Am–F–G–C?
questions.answer: The first ends on V in C major; the second returns to I. In a tonal C-major context that return commonly supplies a stronger sense of arrival.

sections.heading: Move the voices, not just the chord labels
sections.body:
Play C4–E4–G4, then C4–F4–A4. The numbers name octaves using scientific pitch notation, where middle C is C4. The first chord is C major. The second contains F–A–C and is an F-major voicing with C as its lowest note. One pitch stays put, one moves a half step, and one moves a whole step. You changed the harmony without moving every voice a long way.

Voice leading means following the individual lines through a chord progression. A voicing specifies the spacing and order of the notes at one moment. An inversion means a chord tone other than the root is lowest in the relevant chord texture. If a separate bass plays F2 beneath C4–F4–A4, the complete sonority has F at the bottom even though the upper keyboard shape begins on C.

**Worked comparison:** Move each pitch in C4–E4–G4 to the corresponding pitch in C4–F4–A4. The movements are 0, 1 and 2 half steps, for a total of 3. Compare moving all three voices up to F4–A4–C5: each travels 5 half steps, for a total of 15. The smaller total is a useful measure of motion, not proof that the sound is always better. A dramatic leap may be exactly what the phrase needs.

For singers and instruments, check each line's register, contour and breathing or physical demands. Close low-register chords can become muddy; raising inner parts or thinning the texture may help. Common-practice chorale conventions and popular keyboard writing also have different stylistic expectations, so avoid treating one set of part-writing rules as universal.

**Try it:** Use C–F–G–C. Keep a simple bass on chord roots and find upper voicings that retain common tones where useful. Hum each upper line alone. Revise any leap or range problem that distracts from the musical purpose.
sections.visual: Three upper voices connect C major to an F-major voicing. C4 stays, E4 rises to F4, and G4 rises to A4; a separate bass may establish the chord root.

questions.q: What is the total half-step movement from C4–E4–G4 to C4–F4–A4 when corresponding voices connect?
questions.answer: C4 stays: 0. E4 to F4: 1. G4 to A4: 2. Total movement is 3 half steps.

questions.q: Does choosing the least possible motion always produce the best arrangement?
questions.hint: What might the phrase require besides smoothness?
questions.answer: No. Small movement is one useful option, but contour, range, register, independence and expressive intent can justify larger movement.

sections.heading: Make repetition feel intentional
sections.body:
Tap a steady pulse and count 1-and-2-and-3-and-4-and. In a simple 4/4 example, a bar contains four quarter-note beats, and each spoken “and” divides a beat into two equal eighth notes. A quarter note lasts one beat, an eighth note half a beat, a half note two beats, and a dotted half note three beats. A rest occupies time just as a sounding note does.

Meter provides a recurring pattern of strong and weaker positions; rhythm is the particular sequence of durations and attacks. Tempo sets the rate of the pulse. For this course's straight-eighth examples, 96 beats per minute means 96 quarter-note beats per minute. Swing or shuffle changes the subdivision feel and should be specified rather than silently mixed with equal eighth notes.

**Worked bar:** A melody uses two eighth notes, one quarter note, one half note. Its duration is 0.5 + 0.5 + 1 + 2 = 4 beats, so it fits one 4/4 bar. Adding another quarter note would require removing time elsewhere or extending across the bar line; the bar does not grow to fit the phrase.

Syncopation can place an accent on an offbeat or sustain a note across an expected strong position. It works because the listener still has some rhythmic reference. If bass, chords and melody all fill every subdivision with competing accents, the intended pattern may become harder to hear.

**Predict:** Keep the bass on beats 1 and 3, put chord attacks on the offbeats after 2 and 4, and leave a gap before the melody's next phrase. The parts can create motion while preserving space; more attacks are not automatically more energy.

**Try it:** Clap one bar with only two attacks and one with eight. Then repeat the sparse bar under a short melody. Decide which version supports the phrase, and count every rest as carefully as every note.
sections.visual: Eight equal eighth-note slots fill this 4/4 bar. The bass anchors beats 1 and 3 while chord attacks after 2 and 4 create a contrasting rhythmic layer.

questions.q: Do two eighth notes, a quarter note and a half note fit one 4/4 bar?
questions.hint: Add their durations in quarter-note beats.

questions.q: Why can a rest help a phrase feel stronger?
questions.hint: What can the gap make room for or prepare?
questions.answer: A deliberate gap can clarify a rhythmic pattern, give a singer breath, separate phrases or prepare the next entrance. Space is part of the arrangement.

sections.heading: Write a melody that asks and answers
sections.body:
A melody becomes recognisable through relationships that return. Start with a short motive: E4–G4–E4–D4 as four quarter notes over C major. The E–G–E shape repeats a small idea, while D is outside the C-major triad. That D need not be a mistake; it can lead into C in the next bar. Its effect depends on placement, duration and what follows.

Chord tones belong to the current harmony. Non-chord tones do not, but may connect, decorate or delay them. A passing tone can move stepwise between two chord tones. For example, E–F–G over C can connect E and G through F. Not every non-chord tone is a passing tone: its approach, departure and rhythmic role determine the description.

**Build a two-bar phrase:** Over C, use E4 quarter, G4 quarter, E4 quarter, D4 quarter. Over Am, continue C4 quarter, E4 quarter, A4 half. Each bar totals four beats. The first D descends to C at the next bar, while the second bar opens the contour upwards. A note held longer can attract attention even without a leap.

An answering phrase can reuse the rhythm or contour while changing the ending. Keep enough of the motive for recognition, then alter one feature: transpose it, shorten it, extend its final note, or answer it lower. If every note, rhythm and contour changes at once, listeners may hear a new idea rather than a variation.

**Predict:** Repeat a motive twice, then leave a quarter-note rest before the final tonic. The rest can prepare the arrival; it does not have to be filled with another scale run.

**Try it:** Hum your motive without accompaniment. Mark one high point and one breathing place. Play the harmony underneath, then revise one note whose tension does not lead where you intended. Judge the musical effect before labelling every event.
sections.visual: The two-bar idea uses a recurring contour and a longer final note. D in bar 1 leads to C in bar 2; the diagram shows note durations on a beat grid.

questions.q: In E–F–G over a C chord, why can F function as a passing tone?
questions.hint: Look at both its approach and its departure.
questions.answer: F connects the chord tones E and G by stepwise motion. Context and duration still affect how the listener hears it.

questions.q: What should an answering phrase retain if you want it to sound related?
questions.hint: Think beyond simply choosing notes from the same scale.
questions.answer: Retain a recognisable feature such as rhythm, contour or a short interval pattern, then vary another feature to create a purposeful answer.

sections.heading: Arrange an eight-bar song sketch
sections.body:
Build an original eight-bar sketch in C major, 4/4, at a comfortable tempo such as 96 beats per minute. Use this harmonic plan: bar 1 C; bar 2 Am; bar 3 F; bar 4 G; bar 5 C; bar 6 Am; bar 7 F for beats 1–2 and G for beats 3–4; bar 8 C. The first four-bar phrase ends on V. The second returns to I.

Use the following melody as a worked starting point. A quarter note lasts one beat, a half note two, and a dotted half note three. Scientific pitch notation uses C4 for middle C.

- Bar 1: E4 quarter, G4 quarter, E4 quarter, D4 quarter.
- Bar 2: C4 quarter, E4 quarter, A4 half.
- Bar 3: A4 quarter, G4 quarter, F4 half.
- Bar 4: D4 quarter, G4 quarter, B4 half.
- Bar 5: C5 half, G4 quarter, E4 quarter.
- Bar 6: E4 quarter, C4 quarter, A4 half.
- Bar 7: A4 quarter, F4 quarter, G4 quarter, B4 quarter.
- Bar 8: C5 dotted half, quarter rest.

Each bar totals four beats. B4 at the end of bar 4 resolves up to C5 in bar 5; the final B4 likewise leads to C5. These arrivals and the final rest help shape the phrases. The example is a sketch to audition and revise, not a claim that every performer should use this register.

Add a simple bass on chord roots and sparse upper chord voicings. Keep the melody prominent. For a vocal arrangement, transpose into the actual singers' comfortable ranges and leave breathing places; a keyboard sketch is not automatically an idiomatic choir chart.

**Try it:** Perform or hum the melody, then remove half the accompaniment attacks. Compare clarity. Next change just the final chord or the last melody duration and describe the effect. Keep a revision only when it supports the phrase you intended. This course provides notation and reasoning; it does not generate instrumental audio.

questions.q: Does bar 8, C5 dotted half followed by a quarter rest, fill 4/4?
questions.hint: Count the sustained note and the silence.
questions.answer: Yes. The dotted half lasts three beats and the rest one beat, totalling four.

questions.q: What makes the sketch a useful starting point rather than a finished arrangement?
questions.hint: What depends on the actual performers and sound?
questions.answer: Register, voicing, groove, dynamics and breathing must be checked with the performers or instruments. The sketch supplies a coherent form and material to audition and revise.

questions.q: Which pair is a half step within C major?
questions.explain: E–F are adjacent keyboard pitches. The other listed pairs each span a whole step.

questions.q: In G major, what note is scale degree 7?
questions.explain: The major-scale pattern places the seventh one half step below the tonic: F-sharp leads up to G. F-natural changes the scale pattern.

questions.q: You want to transpose a phrase without changing its interval pattern. What should stay constant?
choices: The number of black keys played
questions.explain: Moving every pitch by the same interval preserves the relationships. Keeping letter names or counting black keys does not ensure a transposition.

questions.q: Which notes form the ii triad in C major?
questions.explain: The second scale degree is D. Stacking alternate C-major tones gives D–F–A, a minor triad.

questions.q: In a C-major context, what is a common effect of G7 moving to C?
choices: It guarantees a change to G major
It makes every note a chord tone
questions.explain: G7 functions as V7 in C major and commonly resolves to I. Context still matters; neither a key change nor universal consonance follows automatically.

questions.q: A song loops I–V–vi–IV without a textbook final cadence. Which response is most useful?
choices: Evaluate how the loop supports its phrase, style and intended effect
questions.explain: Function describes useful contextual tendencies. A popular loop can work without following one classical closing pattern.

questions.q: Which upper voice can remain unchanged when C4–E4–G4 moves to C4–F4–A4?
questions.explain: Both voicings contain C4. E moves to F and G to A, so the other two voices change.

questions.q: A separate bass plays F2 under C4–F4–A4. What is the lowest pitch of the complete texture?
questions.explain: The complete texture includes the separate bass, so F2 is lowest. The lowest note of the upper voicing alone is C4.

questions.q: A close low chord sounds muddy beneath a melody. Which change is a reasonable experiment?
choices: Thin or raise inner parts and compare the result
questions.explain: Register and density affect clarity. Thinning or spreading parts is a focused experiment; doubling the congested register may worsen the problem.

questions.q: In this course’s 4/4 examples, how many quarter-note beats does a dotted half note occupy?
questions.explain: A half note occupies two beats; the dot adds half its value, one more beat, for three total.

questions.q: Which placement is an example of syncopation against a clear straight beat?
choices: Playing all notes at the same pitch
An accented attack on the “and” after beat 2
questions.explain: An offbeat accent can create syncopation against an established beat. Pitch alone is unrelated, and the effect relies on rhythmic context.

questions.q: A melody feels crowded. What is the most focused first experiment?
choices: Remove selected accompaniment attacks and compare the phrase
Change every chord and tempo at once
questions.explain: Changing density while preserving other factors lets you hear whether space helps. Simultaneous unrelated changes obscure the cause.

questions.q: Which note is not in a C-major triad?
questions.explain: C major contains C, E and G. D is a scale tone in C major but is not a tone of that triad.

questions.q: Which change most clearly develops a recognisable motive?
choices: Keep its rhythm and vary its ending
questions.explain: Retaining one recognisable feature while changing another creates a relationship the listener can follow. Replacing everything weakens that connection.

questions.q: Your melody fits the key but sounds like an endless scale. What is the best next experiment?
choices: Shape a repeated motive, a high point and a deliberate ending
questions.explain: Key membership alone does not create a phrase. Motive, contour and closure give a line a more specific musical purpose.

questions.q: In the worked sketch, how long does F last in bar 7?
questions.explain: The plan assigns F to beats 1–2 and G to beats 3–4. The bar still totals four beats.

questions.q: What does the final B4 moving to C5 demonstrate in this C-major sketch?
choices: An extra beat added to the bar
questions.explain: B is degree 7 in C major, and C is degree 1. The step supports the planned arrival without changing the bar length or requiring a new key.

questions.q: Which revision process produces the clearest comparison?
choices: Change one musical feature, perform both versions and compare the intended effect
Change tempo, key and every voicing together
Keep only whichever version has more notes
Add parts until all rests disappear
questions.explain: A controlled comparison lets you hear why a revision helps. Note count alone and many simultaneous changes do not identify the musical cause.

sections.title: Hear a home note before naming the chords
bullets: Tonic: a tonal centre is a point of reference, not just the first note
Scale degrees: numbers describe notes relative to that centre
Major scale: whole and half steps create a reusable pattern
Intervals: describe the distance between notes
Experiment: change the ending while keeping the phrase unchanged
sections.notes: Try the sound before the label. Establish C as home, then compare an ending on C with an ending on B. Scale degrees name a relationship to that home. The major-scale step pattern lets you carry the same relationships into another key. Transposition preserves intervals; changing only selected pitches may change the musical idea.
sections.visual: C major has half steps between E–F and B–C. The spacing of the degree markers shows whole and half steps; the numbers describe relationships to C.

sections.title: Give a progression somewhere to go
bullets: Triads: stack alternate scale tones to build three-note chords
Roman numerals: uppercase major and lowercase minor in this course
Function: tonic, predominant and dominant describe common tonal roles
Cadence: the ending of a phrase shapes its sense of arrival
Style: useful tendencies are not universal composition rules
sections.notes: Chords become more informative when you hear their relationships. In C major, I is C, vi is A minor, IV is F and V is G. Compare stopping on the dominant with returning to the tonic. Use the contrast as a writing choice, while remembering that genre and phrasing can change the effect.
sections.visual: In C major, the same chords can be labelled by name and by scale-degree role. The final move from G to C is one common dominant-to-tonic arrival.

sections.title: Move the voices, not just the chord labels
bullets: Voicing: the same chord tones can occupy different registers and orders
Common tones: hold a shared note when it serves the phrase
Economy: compare small inner-voice moves with larger leaps
Bass role: a bass note can establish the root beneath an inversion
Independence: preserve audible parts and comfortable ranges
sections.notes: Follow three lines rather than jumping between chord names. C can stay while E rises to F and G rises to A. That creates a new harmony with little motion. Then add the bass and check the whole texture, because an upper shape’s lowest note is not necessarily the lowest note the listener hears.
sections.visual: Three upper voices connect C major to an F-major voicing. C4 stays, E4 rises to F4, and G4 rises to A4; a separate bass may establish the chord root.

sections.title: Make repetition feel intentional
bullets: Meter: group pulses so rhythmic placement has a reference
Duration: quarter notes, eighth notes and rests occupy time
Syncopation: emphasise an offbeat or carry sound across an expected accent
Groove: coordinate parts through a shared timing pattern
Space: leave deliberate gaps for melody, breath and contrast
sections.notes: Count the time, including silence. Eight equal eighth-note slots fit a simple 4/4 bar, but each part does not need an attack in every slot. Let one part establish the pulse and another answer it. Compare a sparse version with a busy one before deciding which feels more alive.
sections.visual: Eight equal eighth-note slots fill this 4/4 bar. The bass anchors beats 1 and 3 while chord attacks after 2 and 4 create a contrasting rhythmic layer.

sections.title: Write a melody that asks and answers
bullets: Motive: a short recognisable idea can return with variation
Chord tones: use harmonic support without restricting every note
Passing motion: connect stable tones with purposeful non-chord tones
Contour: plan a high point and a place to settle
Phrasing: breath, rests and endings make the line feel intentional
sections.notes: A phrase needs identity and direction. Our first bar has a small recurring contour; D then leads into C, and the next bar opens up to a longer A. Reuse a feature when you answer the phrase. The point is to make the listener recognise an idea and hear what changed.
sections.visual: The two-bar idea uses a recurring contour and a longer final note. D in bar 1 leads to C in bar 2; the diagram shows note durations on a beat grid.

sections.title: Arrange an eight-bar song sketch
bullets: Form: plan two four-bar phrases with different endings
Harmony: give each bar a clear chord and count changes within bars
Melody: preserve a motive while shaping a peak and resolution
Arrangement: assign bass, harmony and melody distinct jobs
Revision: compare one controlled change at a time
sections.notes: The sketch now has eight counted bars, an opening phrase and an answer. Follow B into C at each arrival, and count the final rest. Add parts with distinct jobs rather than doubling everything. Then audition one change at a time. A good arrangement grows from hearing the effect of a choice.
sections.visual: Two four-bar phrases share a harmonic outline. The first ends on G; the second uses a split F/G bar and settles on C with a final rest.

enrichment.audioTitle: Music Theory for Songwriting & Arrangement — think it through

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: You can know every note in a scale and still struggle to write a memorable phrase. Start with a musical home, then shape harmony, rhythm and individual voices into an original eight-bar sketch.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: What should I be able to do by the end?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Write and revise an eight-bar melody with a simple arrangement

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Does calling C home mean every tune must start on C?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: No. The surrounding harmony and phrases establish a tonal centre; the opening pitch can be another degree.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Why do I need F-sharp when I move the C-major pattern to G?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: The major-scale distances must remain the same. F-sharp sits a half step below G; F-natural does not.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Are Roman numerals just another way to spell chord names?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: They also show relationships to a key. The same I–vi–IV–V pattern can move to another tonic while keeping its harmonic outline.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Must every song end V to I?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: No. That is one strong tonal arrival. Loops, modal music and other styles can organise expectation differently.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: If the notes belong to the chord, why care about their order?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Order and register change the voicing, the individual lines and the clarity of the texture.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Do smooth lines mean I should never leap?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: No. Compare the options against the phrase. Economy helps, but range, contour and expressive purpose also matter.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: If every part plays more notes, will the groove improve?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Not necessarily. Shared timing and deliberate gaps can make a pattern clearer than constant competing attacks.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Can I ignore rests when checking a bar?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: No. Rests occupy measured time and help define both the phrase and its breathing space.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: If D is outside the C chord, should I delete it?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Not automatically. It can create useful movement into C. Examine the approach, duration and resolution.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Why does a technically correct scale run feel unmemorable?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: It may lack a recognisable motive, contrast or destination. Give the line a shape and leave space for its ending.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Is this ready to hand directly to a choir?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: It is a keyboard-style song sketch. A choir version needs suitable ranges, voice independence, text and breathing planned for the actual singers.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: How do I know which revision is better?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Perform or hum both versions with one feature changed. Keep the version that better supports the intended phrase and clarity.
